title: BACE: Equipment & Experimental Design - BACE - Experimental Design & Data Analysis
subject: BACE

questions.q: In a spectrophotometry experiment, what is the primary purpose of a 'blank' sample?
options: To calibrate the wavelength accuracy of the machine
To measure the absorbance of the analyte of interest
To increase the sensitivity of the detector
To zero the absorbance reading by accounting for the solvent and reagents
questions.explain: A blank contains everything in the sample except the analyte of interest. It is used to zero the instrument ($A=0$), ensuring that the measured absorbance is due solely to the analyte and not the solvent or cuvette.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Which of the following describes a **Negative Control** in a PCR experiment?
options: A sample containing DNA known to have the target sequence
A reaction mix with water substituted for the DNA template
A sample run at a different temperature to test robustness
A replicate of the experimental sample
questions.explain: A negative control (often 'No Template Control' or NTC) contains reagents but no target DNA. If amplification occurs, it indicates contamination.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: According to legal standards for Lab Notebooks, how should an error be corrected?
options: Use white-out or correction fluid to cover the mistake completely
Tear out the page and rewrite the data on a fresh page
Draw a single line through the error, then initial and date the correction
Scribble over the error until it is illegible
questions.explain: GLP (Good Laboratory Practice) requires that original data remain legible. Errors must be crossed out with a single line, corrected, initialed, and dated to maintain an audit trail.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: A student measures the absorbance of a solution three times and gets: 0.45, 0.46, and 0.45. The true value is 0.80. How would you describe these results?
options: High accuracy, low precision
High accuracy, high precision
Low accuracy, high precision
Low accuracy, low precision
questions.explain: The values are very close to each other (high precision/reproducibility) but far from the true value of 0.80 (low accuracy).
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Which of the following best defines **Principal Component Analysis (PCA)**?
options: A method to sequence DNA fragments rapidly
A statistical technique used to reduce the dimensionality of large datasets while preserving variance
A protocol for validating autoclave sterility
A calculation for determining the molarity of a solution
questions.explain: PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique that transforms a large set of variables into a smaller one (principal components) that still contains most of the information (variance) in the large set.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: In an experiment testing the effect of temperature on enzyme activity, what is the **Independent Variable**?
options: The rate of the reaction
The temperature
The concentration of the enzyme
The pH of the buffer
questions.explain: The independent variable is the one manipulated by the researcher (Temperature). The dependent variable is the response measured (Rate of reaction).
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Which statistical value represents the dispersion or spread of a dataset relative to its mean?
options: Median
Mode
Standard Deviation
P-value
questions.explain: Standard Deviation measures the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values. The Median and Mode are measures of central tendency.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: What is the definition of **Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR)** regarding 'Fabrication'?
options: Using another person's ideas without credit
Making up data or results and recording/reporting them
Manipulating research materials so the research is not accurately represented
Honest error in data entry
questions.explain: Fabrication is defined by the ORI as 'making up data or results'. Falsification (option c) is manipulating data, and Plagiarism (option a) is stealing ideas.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: When performing a t-test, a p-value of 0.03 implies:
options: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% chance the results are due to random error
The results are not statistically significant
The experiment failed
questions.explain: A p-value measures the probability of observing the data (or something more extreme) assuming the null hypothesis is true. $p < 0.05$ is typically considered statistically significant, meaning we reject the null hypothesis.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of **systematic error**?
options: Reading a meniscus slightly differently each time due to eye fatigue
A pipetman that consistently delivers 98 $\mu$L instead of 100 $\mu$L
Fluctuations in room temperature affecting reaction rate
Spilling a small amount of sample
questions.explain: Systematic error is a consistent, repeatable error associated with faulty equipment or a flawed experiment design. It shifts measurements in one direction (bias). Random error (a, c) fluctuates in both directions.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Why are **biological replicates** important in an experiment?
options: To test the pipetting accuracy of the researcher
To account for natural variation between different organisms or biological samples
To ensure the instrument is calibrated correctly
To use up extra reagents before they expire
questions.explain: Biological replicates involve biologically distinct samples (e.g., cells from different animals). They capture biological variation, whereas technical replicates (same sample measured multiple times) capture measurement noise.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: What constitutes a **Positive Control** in an antibiotic susceptibility test?
options: Bacteria plated on media with no antibiotic
Bacteria known to be resistant to the antibiotic
Sterile media with no bacteria
Bacteria known to be sensitive to the antibiotic treated with the antibiotic
questions.explain: A positive control ensures the test is capable of producing a positive result. In this context, using bacteria known to be sensitive ensures the antibiotic is active and the method works. (Option 'a' is a growth control, often also called a positive control for growth, but 'd' is the control for the *antibiotic's effect*).
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: You perform a Q-test and determine that a data point is a statistical outlier. What is the ethical way to handle this?
options: Delete it and pretend it never happened
Keep it in the dataset but note it as an outlier with statistical justification
Change the value to the average of the other points
Repeat the experiment until that specific point matches the others
questions.explain: Data should not be arbitrarily deleted. If a statistical test (like Grubbs' or Q-test) identifies an outlier, it can be excluded from analysis if noted and justified, but the original data must be preserved in the notebook.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Which plot type is most appropriate for determining the linearity of a standard curve?
options: Pie Chart
Scatter Plot with regression line
Bar Graph
Histogram
questions.explain: A scatter plot allows you to plot Concentration (X) vs Absorbance (Y) and fit a linear regression line ($y=mx+b$) to check linearity ($R^2$ value).
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: A 'Double-Blind' study design is used to:
options: Prevent the subjects from knowing which group they are in
Prevent both the subjects and the researchers from knowing group assignments, reducing bias
Ensure the statistics are calculated twice
Test two variables simultaneously
questions.explain: Double-blind studies prevent both observer bias (researcher subconsciously influencing results) and subject bias (placebo effect).
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Using the Beer-Lambert Law ($A = \epsilon l c$), calculate the concentration ($c​$) if Absorbance ($A​$) = 0.5, path length ($l​$) = 1 cm, and molar absorptivity ($\epsilon$) = 5000 $\text{M}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$.
questions.explain: Rearrange the formula: $$c = \frac{A}{\epsilon \times l}$$ ​$$c = \frac{0.5}{5000 \times 1}$$ ​$$c = 0.0001 \text{ M} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ M}$$.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: Which logic error involves assuming that because two variables are correlated, one must cause the other?
options: Selection Bias
Post hoc ergo propter hoc (Correlation implies Causation)
Confirmation Bias
Sampling Error
questions.explain: This is the 'Correlation does not imply causation' fallacy. Two variables might be correlated due to a third confounding variable, not a direct causal link.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA), the First Principal Component (PC1) accounts for:
options: The least amount of variance in the data
The largest possible variance in the data
Only the experimental errors
The correlation between the first two variables
questions.explain: PC1 is the direction in the data space that captures the maximum variance. PC2 captures the next highest variance orthogonal to PC1.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: What is the result of 'Confirmation Bias' in experimental analysis?
options: Searching for or interpreting information in a way that confirms one's preexisting hypotheses
Collecting too much data
Using controls that are too strict
Randomly selecting samples
questions.explain: Confirmation bias is the tendency to favor data that supports your belief while ignoring or discounting data that contradicts it.
questions.subject: BACE

questions.q: If a technician fails to maintain a 'Chain of Custody' for a forensic sample, what is the consequence?
options: The sample cannot be used in legal proceedings
The sample will degrade faster
The experiment must be done in a fume hood
The results will be more accurate
questions.explain: Chain of Custody is the documentation trail tracking the handling of a sample. If broken, the integrity of the sample is compromised, and it is typically inadmissible in court or legal contexts.
